# MC 451 Assignments

**Every assignment in this course, grouped by phase, with what it asks for and when it is due.**

Each assignment shows a short description. Open the section under it for what to submit and the printable rubric, which lists what to include, how long, and what earns full credit.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## How to turn work in

**Submit everything in Blackboard**, under the assignment for that week. Keep your work in your course workspace and commit it to GitHub as usual for the backup and the history, but **committing is not submitting**: grading happens from the Blackboard submission. Two assignments also ask you to paste a GitHub link into the submission; the link goes in the submission, it does not replace it.

Everything is due at **11:59 PM** on the **Friday** listed.

Submissions are **unlimited**. If you upload the wrong file, or want to revise before the deadline, submit again.

**AI-use log:** where an assignment asks for it, the AURA Lab R Companion's output (its setup check, its error explanations, and any code its menus write) is not AI use and is not logged; Copilot is, including any answer Copilot gives using the Companion's tools.
:::


## Every assignment is a part of the paper

Almost nothing here is submitted and then finished. Each assignment builds a component the next one
consumes, and the White Paper is those components assembled and argued.

## Phase III: The Builder {#phase-iii-the-builder}

*Operationalization.* Turn concepts into an instrument a stranger could apply. [Phase page](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/modules/03_builder/?edition=mc451)

### CITI Ethics Certification {#citi-ethics-certification}

**25 points. Due Friday, September 25, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 5)*

Complete the CITI Program's Social and Behavioral Research training and submit your completion certificate. It is due early because it gates the human-subjects reasoning you apply for the rest of the term.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>Full requirements</summary>

**What you submit:** one PDF, the completion certificate as CITI issues it. Do not retype it, screenshot it, or submit the completion report in place of the certificate.

**Requirements**

1. The course completed is **Social and Behavioral Research**, the student version. It is not Responsible Conduct of Research, which does not satisfy this.
2. The institution on the certificate reads **Southern Illinois University Edwardsville**.
3. Your name on the certificate matches your enrolled name.
4. The completion date falls on or before the due date.
5. The certificate carries its verification ID.

**How it is graded.** 5 points per item above. It is a checklist, so a certificate that meets all five earns 25 and one that names the wrong course earns 0 on item 1 regardless of effort.

**Where it comes from.** Session 5 and Chapter 3. **What it feeds:** every later decision about what your data is and whether the people in it needed to consent.

**How this loses points.** Taking Responsible Conduct of Research by mistake is the single most common failure; it appears near the Social and Behavioral course in the CITI menu. Starting it the night before is the second: the modules take two to three hours and the site does not save partial quizzes indefinitely.

</details>

### Annotated Manuscript {#annotated-manuscript}

**25 points. Due Friday, September 25, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 5)*

Find and annotate one peer-reviewed research article related to your topic, then say what it means for your project.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>Full requirements</summary>

**What you submit:** one PDF of the article carrying your highlights and comments, plus a one-page document holding items 2 through 8 below. Two files, or one file if your annotations and notes are in the same PDF.

**Requirements**

1. The article is **peer reviewed** and reports original research. A trade piece, a magazine feature, or a literature review with no data of its own does not qualify.
2. **The gap the authors claim**, in one or two sentences: what they say was missing before their study.
3. **The theoretical framework**, named. If the article uses none, write that it uses none, which is itself a finding.
4. **The method**, with the unit of analysis, the sample and how the key construct was measured.
5. **The finding**, in one sentence, with the **effect size and the sample size** if the article reports them. If it reports neither, say so.
6. **The limitation the authors admit**, and one they do not.
7. **A connection statement**, 100 to 150 words: what this article gives your project, and what it leaves for you to do.
8. A full **reference** for the article, in the citation style you will use for the White Paper.

**How it is graded.** Items 2 through 6 are 3 points each. The connection statement is 5. The reference and the peer-reviewed requirement are 5 between them.

**Where it comes from.** Session 7 and Chapter 4. **What it feeds:** the Project Prospectus, which rests on gaps you can only name from articles you have read this way.

**How this loses points.** Summarizing the article instead of extracting these six things is the usual one: a good summary that never names the gap scores low. Choosing an article because it shares your topic rather than your design is the other; a survey about streaming helps you less than a content analysis of anything.

</details>

### Topic Selection and Research Questions {#topic-selection-and-research-questions}

**25 points. Due Friday, October 2, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 6)*

Commit to a topic and write the questions your study will answer.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>Full requirements</summary>

**What you submit:** one document, roughly one page.

**Requirements**

1. **A topic statement** of two to three sentences naming the phenomenon, the population and the context.
2. **One to three research questions or hypotheses**, numbered. Three is a maximum, not a target.
3. **Why that form**, two to three sentences. Write **hypotheses** (H1, H2, each stated as a directional relationship between two variables) when a theory predicts the direction, and name the theory and what it predicts. Write **research questions** when you are describing or exploring, or when the literature will not support a direction. Neither form is the better answer. An unjustified hypothesis and a question that ducks a clear theoretical prediction lose the same points.
4. **A variable preview**: for each question, name what you would measure and on which unit. Two columns is enough.
5. **A justification**, 100 to 150 words, of why the answer would matter to someone who is not you.
6. **The five-criteria check** for criteria 1 through 4, one line per criterion per question. Criterion 5 is what your justification above already answers, so do not write it twice.

**How it is graded.** Topic 3, questions or hypotheses 6, why that form 3, variable preview 5, why it matters 4, five-criteria check 4.


**Where it comes from.** Sessions 9 and 10, Chapters 5 and 6. **What it feeds:** the Prospectus a week later, which is these questions with a method attached.

**How this loses points.** Submitting a topic where a question was asked is the most common failure: "parasocial interaction on Twitch" is a subject, not a question. Writing five questions is the next, because it usually means none of them has been chosen.

**The five criteria, in full**

**Run every question past these before you submit it:**

1. **Specific.** Name the platform, specify the outcome, bound the population. "How does
   social media influence politics?" leaves all three undefined.
2. **Measurable.** Some concepts resist operationalization. "Do authentic streamers build
   better communities?" cannot be studied until *authentic* and *better* become something
   you can record.
3. **Answerable within your constraints.** Decades of data or hundreds of interviews is
   not a semester project.
4. **Not already answered.** Your literature review tells you whether the question is
   genuinely open.
5. **It matters.** A question can be answerable and still be trivia.

Two of these you can check yourself. **Not already answered** and **it matters** are
judgments you make from your reading, and the check asks you to state the judgment, not
to prove it.

</details>

### Project Prospectus {#project-prospectus}

**25 points. Due Friday, October 9, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 7)*

Put the whole study on one page.

The [Project Prospectus template](mc451-prospectus-template.qmd) goes through each section with its points, the checks that cost points on Topic Selection, and a weaker and a stronger example.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>Full requirements</summary>

**What you submit:** one document, about one page, roughly 250 to 400 words. Seven headed sections.

**Worked example:** [Project Prospectus worked example (PDF)](resources/examples/MC451-example-project-prospectus.pdf). A finished submission, so you can see the form before you write yours.

**Requirements**

1. **A descriptive title** that hints at your key variables.
2. **Research questions or hypotheses**, one to three, carried over from last week and revised if the reading changed them.
3. **A theoretical framework**, two to three sentences: which lens, and what it predicts you will see.
4. **The gap**, two to three sentences, resting on the sources you annotated rather than on an assertion that nobody has studied this.
5. **A method overview**, three to four sentences: unit of analysis, where the data comes from, roughly how much of it, and how you will measure the key construct.
6. **The expected contribution**, one to two sentences.
7. **A rough timeline** to the end of term, by assignment rather than by week.

**How it is graded.** Four points each for questions, theory, gap and method. Three each for title and contribution. Three for the timeline.

**Where it comes from.** Session 11 and Chapter 6. **What it feeds:** everything. The Definitions Practice operationalizes the constructs named here, and the codebook implements them.

**How this loses points.** Writing more than a page is the commonest, and it is a diagnostic rather than a formatting complaint: if you cannot state the project on one page you do not yet understand it well enough to begin. Naming a theory in the framework section and never using it again is the other.

**What a prospectus is.** Roughly one page: what you are studying, why it matters, and
how you will do it. The model prospectus in Chapter 6 runs about 250 words. It is a
diagnostic, not busywork: if you cannot state the project clearly on one page, you do
not yet understand it well enough to begin.

**The six components, with the length each should run:**

| Component | Length |
|---|---|
| Descriptive title hinting at key variables | one line |
| Research questions or hypotheses | 1 to 3, not 10 |
| Theoretical framework | 2 to 3 sentences |
| Gap in the literature | 2 to 3 sentences |
| Method overview | 3 to 4 sentences |
| Expected contribution | 1 to 2 sentences |

Draft all six, even badly, then cut.

</details>

### Codebook and Qualitative Memo {#codebook-and-qualitative-memo}

**50 points. Due Friday, October 23, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 9)*

Build the instrument, and write down what watching taught you. The qualitative reading looks different for every project, depending on your platform and your variables, and it is how you build and solidify the categories, definitions, and edge rules of your quantitative codebook.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** the codebook and a 200 to 300 word qualitative memo, as two documents or one document with two headed parts, uploaded to Blackboard under Codebook and Qualitative Memo.

**Length:** The codebook 1,500 to 3,000 words and the memo 200 to 300 words. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/MC451-501-AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [Codebook and Qualitative Memo rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC451-rubric-codebook-and-qualitative-memo.pdf). It lists the six parts of the codebook, what the memo has to show, and the points for each.

**Worked example:** [Codebook and Qualitative Memo worked example (PDF)](resources/examples/MC451-example-codebook-and-qualitative-memo.pdf). A finished submission, so you can see the form before you write yours.

**Template:** [Codebook and Qualitative Memo template (Quarto .qmd)](resources/templates/MC451-codebook-template.qmd) or [the same template (Word .docx)](resources/templates/MC451-codebook-template.docx). Use it directly as your `codebook/codebook.qmd` or as inspiration for your own layout.

</details>

### Sampling Plan and Pilot {#sampling-plan-and-pilot}

**75 points. Due Friday, November 6, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 11)*

Decide what you will code, then prove the codebook survives contact with it. The pilot is your first quantitative pass: the codebook your close reading built, frozen and applied to real items, with a check on your own consistency.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** one document with two parts, the sampling plan and the pilot, plus your coded pilot data as a spreadsheet or CSV, uploaded to Blackboard under Sampling Plan and Pilot. Optional: the R Companion's **Reliability grid** takes your pass 1 and pass 2 codes, saves them as a CSV, and writes the `v2v::reliability()` call into your script. To code the pilot items in VS Code instead of a spreadsheet, **AURA: Open the data viewer** opens your CSV in a grid where you add your coding columns and code each row; your codes save to `data/derived/`, the original file is never changed, and **Insert rebuild code** writes the lines that join the codes back on. Excel and Google Sheets still work.

**Length:** 700 to 1,200 words across the plan and the pilot write-up, plus 10 to 20 coded items in the spreadsheet. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/MC451-501-AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [Sampling Plan and Pilot rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC451-rubric-sampling-plan-and-pilot.pdf). It lists each part of the plan and the pilot with its points, and carries the table for sizing your corpus.

</details>

### Data Wrangling in R {#data-wrangling-in-r}

**50 points. Due Friday, November 13, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 12)*

Build the analysis-ready table from the raw one.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** your script and the exported dataset, saved as `twitch_analysis.RDS` because Describing Data and Inferencing Data both read that file, uploaded to Blackboard under Data Wrangling in R. You may build steps with the R Companion's Data menu. What it writes lands in your script, and the script is what is graded. Export to RDS, not CSV.

**Length:** One script of 40 to 120 lines, comments included, plus the 30-row coding form. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/MC451-501-AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [Data Wrangling in R rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC451-rubric-data-wrangling-in-r.pdf). It lists the eight steps the script carries and the points for each.

</details>

### Describing Data in R {#describing-data-in-r}

**75 points. Due Friday, November 20, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 13)*

Say what is in the data before you test anything.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** your script or Quarto document and the rendered output carrying the figures, uploaded to Blackboard under Describing Data in R. Optional: the Describe group of the R Companion's **Write R code** writes frequency tables, crosstabs with proportions, grouped summaries, and the bar chart, histogram, histogram comparing two groups, line chart over time, and boxplot in `theme_v2v()`, each chart saved with `ggsave()` and carrying an alt-text line marked YOUR TURN. The alt text and the interpretation stay your own writing.

**Length:** 300 to 600 words of your own writing (interpretation and alt text), not counting code or output. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/MC451-501-AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [Describing Data in R rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC451-rubric-describing-data-in-r.pdf). It lists the tables, numbers, figures, and interpretation it asks for, and the points for each.

</details>

### Inferencing Data in R {#inferencing-data-in-r}

**100 points. Due Friday, December 4, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 15)*

Test four relationships, one per test, and report how big each is.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** your script or Quarto document and the rendered output, uploaded to Blackboard under Inferencing Data in R. Optional: the Test group of the R Companion's **Write R code** writes the four tests for your settings-block variables, the plain R call first and the `v2v` wrapper after it as a check, and its **APA numbers to check your sentence** prints a test's numbers in APA form. The hypotheses, the reason for each test, the four reports, and the interpretation are your own writing.

**Length:** 500 to 900 words of your own writing (hypotheses, the four reports, interpretation and the limits paragraph), not counting code or output. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/MC451-501-AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [Inferencing Data in R rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC451-rubric-inferencing-data-in-r.pdf). It lists each step from the four hypotheses to what the results do not license, and the points for each.

</details>

## Phase V: The Publisher {#phase-v-the-publisher}

*Inference and Publication.* Test the relationship and publish the result. [Phase page](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/modules/05_publisher/?edition=mc451)

### White Paper {#white-paper}

**250 points. Due Friday, December 18, 11:59 PM.**

The final deliverable: your study written up in IMRaD, reporting the quantitative results from your coded sample along with the qualitative themes from the close reading that built your codebook, rendered to PDF and published to the web.

**Dated step, Friday, December 4, 11:59 PM:** push the full coded dataset and a re-code of a fresh subsample to your project repository. The stability figure in Methods earns its points only if that commit is dated on or before December 4; the rubric carries the subsample rule. Nothing about your analysis is due that day.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** two things, both required: the paper as a PDF, and the live URL of your GitHub Pages site. Upload the PDF and paste the URL into the Blackboard submission for White Paper; one without the other is incomplete.

**Length:** 3,500 to 5,000 words from the introduction through the reflection. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/MC451-501-AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [White Paper rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC451-rubric-white-paper.pdf). It lists what each section carries, the source and citation requirements, and the points for each.

</details>
